sentences.t: 2016: Groww starts in Bengaluru, founded by former Flipkart employees (Reuters).
The company was incorporated in 2018 as Billionbrains Garage Ventures, per its corporate identity number; Groww's own IPO page uses 2018.
March 2023: 5.37 million active clients on the NSE, a 15.09% share of the exchange's active base (prospectus).
FY23 to FY25: revenue from operations compounds at 84.9% a year (prospectus).
June 2025: 12.58 million NSE active clients, 26.27% share.
Roughly one in three new SIPs in India that month was created on Groww; it held 18.5% of all active SIPs (prospectus, citing AMFI data).
October 2025: acquires Fisdom, a wealth-management platform (shareholders' letter).
4-7 November 2025: IPO of ₹6,632 crore at ₹95-100 a share, subscribed 17.6 times (Groww IPO page).
12 November 2025: lists at ₹112, up 12%, and climbs to ₹124 on debut, valuing the company at ₹761 billion, about $8.6 billion, above listed peers Motilal Oswal and Angel One (Reuters).
November 2025: first listed quarter, Q2 FY26, shows the regulatory squeeze: revenue down 9.5% year on year (Economic Times).
March quarter 2026: the rebound.
Total income ₹1,536 crore, up 81% year on year; profit ₹686 crore, a 44.7% margin (shareholders' letter).
September 2026: adds over 1 lakh NSE active clients in the month, keeping the industry lead as the total base reaches 4.61 crore (NSE data via Startup Spotlight India).
Groww is a direct-to-customer investment platform: stocks, derivatives, mutual funds, bonds, IPOs, margin funding and personal loans in one app (prospectus).
Broking produced 84.5% of FY25 revenue, and management has been widening the mix since.

By the March 2026 quarter, equity derivatives (futures and options on stocks and indices) were 54.6% of total income, with stocks, commodities, margin trading, credit and treasury income making up the rest (shareholders' letter).
Product attach is the engine: 72% of active users trade stocks, 60% use mutual funds, 10% trade equity derivatives (letter, Q4 FY26).
Commodity derivatives reached 393,000 active traders, up 53.8% in the quarter, still only a 2.4% attach rate, which is why management calls it early.
The credit business, loans distributed for partner banks plus some on Groww's own balance sheet, contributed 4.1% of consolidated profit in Q4 FY26.
Across FY23, FY24, FY25 and the June 2025 quarter, between 81% and 84% of new customers arrived organically, without paid marketing (prospectus).
Of users who completed three years on the platform, 77.7% remained.
Transacting users opened the app often: a daily-to-monthly active ratio of about 56% in FY25.
Cohorts deepen with age: users acquired in early FY22 held 5.36 times more assets per user by FY25, generated 1.86 times more revenue per user, and 53% of them used two or more products (prospectus).
The listed-company wrinkle: acquisition cost is rising as Groww spends on brand.
Customer acquisition cost reached ₹1,374 in H1 FY26, against ₹796 a year earlier, after branding campaigns (Economic Times on Q2 FY26).

The company's own framing splits spending into "cost to serve" (technology and transaction charges, 14.7% of Q4 FY26 revenue), "cost to grow" (marketing, 8.5%) and "cost to operate" (mostly employees, 18.8%), leaving an EBITDA margin of 66.1% on the platform before the Fisdom and GrowwMF losses.

SEBI (the securities market regulator) tightened derivatives rules in October 2024, and the impact was direct: Groww's active broking users fell from 7.24 million in Q1 FY25 to 6.12 million in Q1 FY26 (prospectus).
A "true-to-label" circular then cut revenue per derivatives order (Economic Times).

The September 2025 quarter captured the combined effect: revenue fell 9.5% year on year while profit rose 12%, and the company disclosed that adjusting for a one-time incentive reversal, profit too would have declined 12-13%.
Industry-wide, NSE active users shrank from 50.2 million in January 2025 to 45.3 million by September 2025; Groww's fell less, from 13.2 to 11.9 million, so share kept rising through the shrink.

The response is the diversification visible in the numbers: margin trading book up 22% in a quarter when indices fell 16-17% and the industry book contracted 7%; commodity derivatives scaling; credit contributing to profit.

The two loss-makers are deliberate: Fisdom lost ₹10.2 crore and the GrowwMF fund house lost ₹21.4 crore in Q4 FY26, with Fisdom expected to be profitable in FY28 and GrowwMF needing five to six times its current assets under management to break even (management's statements in the letter).
FY26 closed with revenue from operations of ₹4,645 crore and profit of ₹2,083 crore, audited and consolidated (Q1 FY27 filing).
The newest quarter, Q1 FY27 ended June 2026, brought revenue of ₹1,501 crore, up 66% year on year, and profit of ₹735 crore, up 94%.

Platform scale at March 2026: 21.6 million total transacting users, 16.7 million active users, ₹3.0 trillion in customer assets, up 36% year on year, and ₹25,000 crore of net inflows in the March quarter alone.
Customer assets dipped 1.1% in that quarter despite inflows, because falling markets marked down existing holdings; the company publishes the split.

The cleanest read on the Groww thesis: in a year when the industry's active base shrank, Groww's share of SIP (systematic investment plan, a recurring mutual fund investment) inflows rose from 12.1% to 15.7%, of retail cash-market turnover from 12.3% to 14.0%, of retail derivatives premium turnover from 6.8% to 10.6%, and of the margin-funding book from 0.9% to 2.7% (letter).
Gaining share in a shrinking market is how a platform grows through a regulatory squeeze; it is also why the squeeze's cost lands on competitors first.
Pair this with yesterday's Zerodha teardown and the two strategies stand in relief.

Zerodha, private and bootstrapped, earned ₹4,237 crore on ₹8,847 crore of revenue in FY25, but both shrank, revenue down 11.5% and profit down 22.9%, and it holds ₹22,679 crore in cash (RoC filings via Entrackr).
Groww, venture-raised and now listed, earned ₹2,083 crore on ₹4,645 crore in FY26, growing 81% in the final quarter.
The incumbent is bigger, more profitable and contracting; the challenger is half the profit, growing fast, and deploying IPO money into lending and wealth.
Different periods, labelled: Zerodha's figures are FY25, Groww's are FY26.
Same regulator squeezing both core products.
Source: Entrackr on Zerodha's FY25 RoC filing.
Q2 FY27 results, due around November by last year's pattern: does the 66% revenue growth of Q1 hold, and does acquisition cost keep climbing?
The derivatives dependency: 54.6% of total income in Q4 FY26, with SEBI still tightening.
Every new rule has so far shrunk the market faster than Groww's share gains could fully offset.
Margin-funding risk: the MTF book grew 22% in a falling market.
Leveraged books grow fastest into volatility; the March quarter's risk-cost increase, which management flagged, is the line to watch.
Fisdom integration: management says profitability in FY28.
Wealth management is the natural next attach product after stocks and funds.
GrowwMF: the fund house needs five to six times current assets to break even, by management's own estimate.
Watch new fund launches and whether the platform pushes its own funds to its 18.5% SIP share.
